english: Everything was silent. Nobody seemed to be stirring in the house yet. She looked at it, sleeping there in the early sunlight, its windows green and blue with the reflected leaves. The faint thought she was having about Mrs. Ramsay seemed in harmony with this quiet house, this smoke, this fine early-morning air. Faint and unreal, it was amazingly pure and exciting. She hoped nobody would open a window or come out of the house, but that she would be left alone to go on thinking, to go on painting. She turned to her canvas. But pushed by some curiosity, driven by the discomfort of the sympathy she was still holding in, unreleased, she walked a step or two to the end of the lawn to see whether, down there on the beach, she could see that little company setting sail. Down there among the little boats floating on the water, some with their sails furled, some moving slowly away, for it was very calm, there was one a little apart from the others. Its sail was being hoisted at that very moment. She decided that there, in that very distant and entirely silent little boat, Mr. Ramsay was sitting with Cam and James. Now they had got the sail up; now, after a little flagging and hesitation, the sails filled, and, wrapped in deep silence, she watched the boat make its way deliberately past the other boats and out to sea.

Den svage tanke, hun gjorde sig om fru Ramsay, syntes at harmonere med dette stille hus, denne røg, denne fine morgenluft. Svag og uvirkelig som den var, var den forbavsende ren og opildnende. Hun håbede, at ingen ville åbne et vindue eller komme ud af huset, men at hun ville blive ladt alene til at tænke videre, til at male videre. Hun vendte sig mod sit lærred. Men drevet af en nysgerrighed, skubbet af ubehaget ved den medfølelse, hun stadig holdt tilbage, uudløst, gik hun et par skridt hen til enden af plænen for at se, om hun dernede på stranden kunne få øje på det lille selskab, der stak til søs. Dernede blandt de små både, der flød på vandet, nogle med sejlene beslået, nogle langsomt på vej bort, for det var meget stille, var der én lidt for sig selv. Dens sejl blev hejst netop i dette øjeblik. Hun besluttede, at dér, i den fjerne og fuldstændig lydløse lille båd, sad hr. Ramsay sammen med Cam og James. Nu havde de fået sejlet op; nu, efter en smule slappen og tøven, fyldtes sejlene, og indhyllet i dyb stilhed så hun båden bevæge sig besluttsomt forbi de andre både og ud på havet.

english: And what name would she give him? her father kept on. When he was a small boy he had had a dog called Frisk. She’s going to give in, James thought, watching a certain look come over her face, a look he remembered. They look down at their knitting, or something, he thought. Then all at once they look up. He remembered a flash of blue, and then someone sitting with him laughed and gave in, and he was furious. It must have been his mother, he thought, in a low chair, with his father standing over her. He began to hunt through the endless series of impressions that time had laid down on his brain, softly, ceaselessly, leaf upon leaf, fold upon fold: scents, sounds; voices, harsh, hollow, sweet; lights going by, and brooms tapping; the wash and hush of the sea; how a man had marched up and down and stopped dead, standing upright over them. Meanwhile, he noticed, Cam was dabbling her fingers in the water, staring at the shore, saying nothing. No, she won’t give in, he thought; she’s not like that. Well, then, if Cam would not answer, he would leave her alone, Mr. Ramsay decided, and felt in his pocket for a book. But she did want to answer him. She longed, passionately, to shift whatever lay on her tongue and blocked it, and to say, Oh yes, Frisk. I’ll call him Frisk. She even wanted to ask, Was that the dog that found its own way across the moor? But however hard she tried, she could think of nothing like that to say—something fierce and faithful to the compact, yet which would pass her father, without James suspecting, a secret sign of the love she felt for him. For as she dabbled her hand (and just then Macalister’s boy caught a mackerel, and it lay kicking on the bottom of the boat with blood on its gills)—for as she looked at James, who kept his eyes on the sail without any feeling, or now and then glanced at the horizon for a second, she thought: you aren’t exposed to it—this pressure, this split feeling, this extraordinary temptation. Her father was searching his pockets; another second and he would have his book. For nobody drew her more than he did. His hands were beautiful to her, and his feet, and his voice, his words, his hurry, his temper, his strangeness, his passion, the way he would say straight out in front of everybody, we perish, each alone, and his remoteness. (He had opened his book.) But what was still unbearable, she thought, sitting up straight and watching Macalister’s boy pull the hook from another fish’s gills, was that crude blindness and tyranny of his. It had poisoned her childhood and stirred up bitter storms, so that even now she would wake at night shaking with rage, remembering some command of his, some insolence: “Do this,” “Do that”; his domination; his “Submit to me.”
danish_before_fix: Og hvad navn ville hun give den? blev hendes far ved. Da han var en lille dreng, havde han haft en hund, der hed Frisk. Nu giver hun efter, tænkte James, mens han så et vist udtryk brede sig over hendes ansigt, et udtryk han huskede. De ser ned på deres strikketøj eller sådan noget, tænkte han. Så ser de pludselig op. Han huskede et glimt af blåt, og så lo en, der sad sammen med ham, og gav efter, og han blev rasende. Det måtte have været hans mor, tænkte han, i en lav stol, med hans far stående over hende. Han begyndte at lede gennem den endeløse række af indtryk, som tiden havde lagt ned på hans hjerne, blidt, uophørligt, blad på blad, fold på fold: dufte, lyde; stemmer, hårde, hule, bløde; lys der gik forbi, og koste der bankede; havets skvulp og hvisken; hvordan en mand var marcheret op og ned og var standset brat, rejst op over dem. Imens lagde han mærke til, at Cam dyppede fingrene i vandet, stirrede mod kysten og ikke sagde noget. Nej, hun giver ikke efter, tænkte han; sådan er hun ikke. Nå, men hvis Cam ikke ville svare, ville han lade hende være, besluttede hr. Ramsay og famlede i lommen efter en bog. Men hun ville gerne svare ham. Hun længtes, lidenskabeligt, efter at flytte det, der lå på hendes tunge og spærrede, og sige: Åh jo, Frisk. Jeg kalder den Frisk. Hun ville endda spørge: Var det den hund, der fandt hjem over heden på egen hånd? Men hvor hårdt hun end prøvede, kunne hun ikke finde på noget af den slags at sige — noget heftigt og tro mod pagten, men som ville række hendes far, uden at James anede det, et hemmeligt tegn på den kærlighed, hun nærede til ham. For mens hun dyppede sin hånd (og netop da fik Macalisters dreng en makrel, og den lå og sprællede på bunden af båden med blod på gællerne) — for mens hun så på James, som holdt blikket på sejlet uden nogen følelse eller en gang imellem et øjeblik kiggede mod horisonten, tænkte hun: du er ikke udsat for det — dette pres, denne splittede følelse, denne ekstraordinære fristelse. Hendes far søgte i sine lommer; et sekund til, og han ville have sin bog. For ingen drog hende mere end han. Hans hænder var smukke for hende, og hans fødder, og hans stemme, hans ord, hans hastværk, hans hidsighed, hans mærkelighed, hans lidenskab, den måde han midt foran alle sammen kunne sige lige ud, vi omkommer, hver for sig, og hans afsides væsen. (Han havde åbnet sin bog.) Men det, der stadig var uudholdeligt, tænkte hun, mens hun satte sig op og så Macalisters dreng trække krogen ud af en anden fisks gæller, var hans rå blindhed og tyranni. Det havde forgiftet hendes barndom og vakt bitre storme, så hun selv nu kunne vågne om natten og ryste af raseri, når hun huskede et eller andet påbud fra ham, en eller anden uforskammethed: »Gør dét,« »Gør hint«; hans herredømme; hans »Underkast dig mig.«

english: Hares bored Minta, Lily thought. But Minta never gave herself away. She would never say a thing like that about chess in coffeehouses; she was much too self-aware, much too careful. Still, to go on with their story—by now the dangerous stage was behind them. Lily had stayed with them for a while last summer, and the car broke down, and Minta had to pass him his tools. He sat in the road fixing it, and the way she passed him the tools—businesslike, direct, friendly—was proof that all was well now. They were not “in love” anymore. No: he had taken up with another woman, a serious woman who wore her hair in a braid and carried a briefcase (Minta described her with gratitude, almost with admiration). She went to meetings and shared Paul’s views, which had grown more and more pronounced, on taxing land values and on a capital levy. That alliance, far from wrecking the marriage, had put it right. Clearly they were excellent friends, he sitting in the road and she handing him his tools.

Hun ville aldrig sige sådan noget som det om skak på kaffehuse; hun var alt for opmærksom på sig selv, meget for forsigtig. Men for at fortsætte deres historie — nu var det farlige stadie overstået. Lily havde boet hos dem et stykke tid sidste sommer, og bilen var gået i stykker, og Minta havde måttet række ham hans værktøj. Han sad på vejen og reparerede den, og den måde, hun rakte ham værktøjet på — forretningsmæssigt, ligefremt, venskabeligt — var et bevis på, at alt var godt nu. De var ikke »forelskede« mere. Nej: han havde slået sig sammen med en anden kvinde, en alvorlig kvinde, der bar sit hår i en fletning og gik med en dokumenttaske (Minta beskrev hende med taknemlighed, næsten med beundring). Hun gik til møder og delte Pauls synspunkter, som var blevet mere og mere markante, om beskatning af jordværdier og om en kapitalafgift. Den alliance havde, langt fra at ødelægge ægteskabet, bragt det på ret køl. Det var tydeligt, at de var fortrinlige venner, han siddende på vejen og hun rækkende ham sit værktøj.

english: So that was the Rayleys’ story, Lily thought, smiling. She pictured herself telling it to Mrs. Ramsay, who would be eager to hear how the Rayleys had turned out. There would be a little triumph in it for Lily, telling Mrs. Ramsay that the marriage had not succeeded.

english: (All at once, as suddenly as a star slides down the sky, a reddish light seemed to blaze up in her mind; it covered Paul Rayley and poured out from him. It went up like a bonfire lit by savages on some faraway beach to mark a celebration. She heard it roar and crackle. For miles around, the whole sea ran red and gold. A smell like wine was mixed into it and went to her head, because she felt once more her own reckless longing to throw herself off the cliff and drown hunting for a pearl brooch on a beach. And the roar and crackle filled her with fear and disgust and drove her back. It was as if, even while she saw how splendid and powerful it was, she also saw how it fed on the treasure of the house, greedily and disgustingly, and she loathed it. Yet as a spectacle, as a glory, it outshone anything she had ever experienced; year after year it burned like a signal fire on a desert island at the sea’s edge, and you had only to say “in love” for Paul’s fire to leap up again at once, as it did now. Then it died down, and she said to herself with a laugh, “The Rayleys”—how Paul went to coffeehouses and played chess.)

english: Lily looked at the drawing-room step now. Through William’s eyes she saw the shape of a woman, quiet and peaceful, her eyes cast down. She sat lost in thought, pondering (she was wearing gray that day, Lily thought). Her gaze was lowered. She would never raise it. Yes, thought Lily, looking hard, I must have seen her look that way—but not in gray, and not so still, or so young, or so peaceful. The figure came easily enough. She was astonishingly beautiful, William said. But beauty wasn’t everything. Beauty had this price: it came too easily and too completely. It stopped life still—froze it. You forgot the small agitations: the flush, the paleness, some strange twist, some light or shadow that made the face unrecognizable for an instant and yet added something you saw in it ever after. It was simpler to smooth all that away beneath beauty. But what did she look like, Lily wondered, when she clapped her deerstalker hat on her head, or ran across the grass, or scolded Kennedy, the gardener? Who could tell her that? Who could help her?

Hun var forbløffende smuk, sagde William. Men skønhed var ikke alt. Skønhed havde den pris: den kom for let og for fuldstændigt. Den standsede livet — frøs det. Man glemte de små uroligheder: rødmen, bleghed, et eller andet sært spil, et eller andet lys eller en skygge, der gjorde ansigtet ukendeligt et øjeblik og dog føjede noget til, man siden altid så i det. Hvem kunne hjælpe hende?

english: She wanted to walk straight over and say, “Mr. Carmichael!” He would look up kindly, as he always did, out of his vague, smoky green eyes. But you only woke people when you knew what you wanted to tell them. And what she wanted to say was not one thing but everything. Small words that chopped the thought up into pieces said nothing at all. “About life, about death; about Mrs. Ramsay”—no, she thought, you could say nothing to anybody. The urgency of the moment always missed. Words fluttered off to the side and struck inches below the target. Then you gave up, and the idea sank back down, and you turned into what most middle-aged people become: cautious, secretive, with lines between the eyes and a look of permanent anxiety. Because how could you put these feelings of the body into words? How could you express that emptiness there? (She was looking at the drawing-room steps. They looked extraordinarily empty.) It was the body that felt it, not the mind. The physical sensations that came with the bare look of those steps had all at once turned extremely unpleasant. Wanting and not having sent a hardness, a hollowness, a strain right through her body. And then wanting and not having—wanting and wanting—how it wrung the heart, over and over! Oh, Mrs. Ramsay! she cried out without a sound, to that essence sitting by the boat, that abstraction made out of her, that woman in gray—as if to scold her for having gone, and then, having gone, for coming back. Thinking of her had seemed so safe. Ghost, air, nothing, something you could toy with easily and safely at any hour of the day or night—that was what she had been. And then suddenly Mrs. Ramsay reached out her hand and wrung the heart like this. english: And now, little by little, the pain of wanting, and the bitter anger (at being called back just when she believed she would never grieve for Mrs. Ramsay again—had she missed her among the coffee cups at breakfast? Not at all), grew less. What their anguish left behind, as a remedy, was a relief that soothed in itself, and also, more mysteriously, a sense that someone was there—Mrs. Ramsay, freed for a moment of the weight the world had laid on her, lingering lightly beside Lily and then (for this was Mrs. Ramsay in all her beauty) lifting to her forehead a wreath of white flowers and going off with it. Lily squeezed her tubes again and attacked the problem of the hedge. It was odd how clearly she could see Mrs. Ramsay stepping, quick as always, across fields that were soft and purplish in their folds, full of flowers—hyacinths or lilies—among which she vanished. It was a trick of the painter’s eye. For days after hearing of her death, Lily had seen her like this, raising the wreath to her forehead and going off unquestioningly across the fields with her companion, a shadow. The sight, and the phrase, had power to comfort. Wherever she was—painting here in the country, or in London—the vision would come, and her eyes would half close, searching for something to rest the vision on. She would look down the railway carriage, or the bus; take a line from someone’s shoulder or cheek; look at the windows across the way; at Piccadilly strung with lamps at evening. All of it had been part of the fields of death. But there was always something—a face, perhaps, or a voice, or a newsboy calling the evening papers, _Standard, News_—that pushed through, snubbed her, woke her, and demanded, and in the end received, an effort of attention, so that the vision had to be made again and again. Now once more, driven by some instinctive need for distance and for blue, she gazed down at the bay, turning the blue bars of the waves into little hills and the more purple patches into stony fields. And once again, as always, something that didn’t belong startled her. In the middle of the bay was a brown speck. It was a boat—she saw that after a second. But whose? Mr. Ramsay’s, she answered. Mr. Ramsay: the man who had marched past her, aloof, with his hand raised, leading a procession, in those beautiful boots of his, asking for sympathy she had refused to give. By now the boat was halfway across the bay.

english: Then the swirl around her hand died away. The water stopped rushing past; the world was full of small creaks and squeaks. You could hear the waves breaking and lapping at the side of the boat as if they lay at anchor in a harbor. Everything drew very near. James had kept his eyes on the sail until it had become like a person he knew, and now it sagged completely, so they came to a halt, flapping about and waiting for a breeze in the hot sun, miles from land, miles from the Lighthouse. The whole world seemed to stand still. The Lighthouse stopped moving, and the line of the far shore stayed fixed. As the sun grew hotter, they all seemed to draw very close together and to sense one another’s presence, which they had nearly forgotten. Macalister’s fishing line dropped straight down into the water. But Mr. Ramsay kept reading, his legs tucked up under him.

english: The book he was reading was a small, glossy one, its covers speckled like a plover’s egg. Every now and then, as they drifted in that dreadful calm, he turned a page. To James it seemed that every page was turned with a particular gesture meant for him—sometimes assertive, sometimes commanding, sometimes designed to make people feel sorry for him. And the whole time his father was reading and turning those little pages one after another, James was dreading the moment he would look up and say something sharp to him about one thing or another. Why were they hanging about here? he would ask, or something just as unreasonable. And if he does, James thought, I’ll take a knife and strike him to the heart.

english: This old symbol—taking a knife and striking his father to the heart—he had always kept. Only now that he was older, as he sat glaring at his father in helpless fury, it was not the man himself he wanted to kill, not that old man reading. It was the thing that came down on him—perhaps without his knowing: that fierce, sudden harpy with black wings, its claws and beak all hard and cold, which struck and struck at you (he could feel that beak on his bare legs, where it had struck him as a child) and then flew off; and there he was again, an old man, very sad, reading his book. That was what he would kill; that was what he would strike to the heart. Whatever he did with his life—(and he felt he might do anything, as he looked at the Lighthouse and the distant shore)—whether he went into business or a bank, or became a lawyer, or ran some enterprise, that was what he would fight, what he would hunt down and stamp out: tyranny, despotism, as he called it—forcing people to do what they didn’t want to do, taking away their right to speak. How could any of them say, But I won’t, when he said, Come to the Lighthouse. Do this. Fetch me that. The black wings spread; the hard beak tore. And then, a moment later, there he was, sitting reading; and he might look up—you never could tell—perfectly reasonably. He might chat with the Macalisters. He might be pressing a gold coin into the hand of some freezing old woman in the street, James thought; he might be cheering at some fishermen’s sports day; he might be flinging his arms about in excitement. Or he might sit at the head of the table without a word from one end of dinner to the other. Yes, James thought, while the boat slapped and lazed about in the hot sun: there was a wasteland of snow and rock, very lonely and stern; and there, he had begun to feel quite often lately, whenever his father said something that took the others by surprise, were only two sets of footprints—his and his father’s. Only they knew each other. Then what was this terror, this hatred? He turned back among the many leaves the past had folded inside him, peering into the heart of that forest where light and shadow so dapple each other that every shape is warped, and you stumble along, now with the sun in your eyes, now in dark shade. He was searching for an image that would cool his feeling, set it apart, and round it off into something solid. Suppose, then, that when he was a child sitting helpless in his baby carriage, or on somebody’s lap, he had seen a cart crush someone’s foot, without meaning to, innocently? Suppose he had seen the foot first, smooth and whole in the grass; then the wheel; then that same foot, purple and crushed. But the wheel was innocent. And so now, when his father came striding down the hall early in the morning, banging on their doors to get them up to go to the Lighthouse, it came down over his foot, over Cam’s foot, over anyone’s foot. You just sat and watched.

Eller han kunne sidde for bordenden uden et ord fra den ene ende af middagen til den anden. Ja, tænkte James, mens båden klaskede og dovnede i den hede sol: der lå en ødemark af sne og klippe, meget ensom og streng; og der, det var han for nylig begyndt at føle ret ofte, hver gang hans far sagde noget, der overrumplede de andre, var kun to sæt fodspor — hans og hans fars. Han bladrede tilbage blandt de mange blade, som fortiden havde foldet inde i ham, og spejdede ind i hjertet af den skov, hvor lys og skygge pletter hinanden så, at enhver skikkelse bliver forvredet, og man snubler af sted, nu med solen i øjnene, nu i mørk skygge. Man sad bare og så på.

Han bladrede tilbage blandt de mange blade, som fortiden havde foldet inde i ham, og spejdede ind i hjertet af den skov, hvor lys og skygge pletter hinanden så, at enhver skikkelse bliver forvredet, og man snubler af sted, nu med solen i øjnene, nu i mørk skygge. Antag da, at han som barn, hjælpeløs i sin barnevogn eller på en andens skød, havde set en vogn knuse en andens fod, uden at mene det, uskyldigt? Man sad bare og så på.

english: So this was the island, Cam thought, as she trailed her fingers through the waves again. Never before had she seen it from out at sea. So that was how it lay on the water: a dent in its middle, two sharp crags, the sea sweeping in there and stretching away for mile after mile on either side. It was tiny—shaped rather like a leaf standing on its end. So we took a little boat, she thought, and began telling herself an adventure story about escaping from a ship that was going down. But with the sea running through her fingers, and a sprig of seaweed disappearing behind them, she had no wish to tell herself a story in earnest. What she wanted was the feeling of adventure and escape. For as the boat sailed on she was thinking how everything had slipped away, passed, streamed off behind them: her father’s fury over the points of the compass, James’s obstinacy about their compact, her own misery. So what came next? Where were they heading? Out of her hand, icy cold, sunk deep in the sea, a fountain of joy shot up—joy at the change, the escape, the adventure (that she was alive, that she was here). And the drops from this sudden, thoughtless fountain fell here and there on the dark, drowsing shapes in her mind—shapes of a world she had not yet made real, turning in their darkness and catching a spark of light here and there: Greece, Rome, Constantinople. Tiny as it was, like a leaf on end, with the gold-flecked water flowing in and around it, did even that little island, she wondered, have its place in the universe? The old gentlemen in the study could have told her, she thought. Now and then she wandered in from the garden on purpose to catch them at it. There they would be (Mr. Carmichael, perhaps, or Mr. Bankes, very old and very stiff), facing each other in their low armchairs, crackling the pages of _The Times_ in front of them. She would come in from the garden with everything muddled in her head: something someone had said about Christ; a mammoth dug up in a London street; what had the great Napoleon been like? And they would take all this up in their clean hands (their clothes were gray; they smelled of heather), brush the scraps together, turn the paper, cross their knees, and every so often say something very short. As if in a trance, she would take a book off the shelf and stand watching her father write—so evenly, so neatly, from one edge of the page across to the other—coughing a little now and then, or saying something brief to the other old gentleman across from him. And standing there with her book open, she thought: here you could let any thought you had unfold like a leaf in water; and if it did well here, among the smoking old gentlemen and the crackle of _The Times_, then it was right. And as she watched her father writing in his study, she thought (sitting in the boat now) that he was utterly lovable and utterly wise; he was not vain, and he was no tyrant. english: So a great deal depends, then, Lily Briscoe thought as she looked at the sea—hardly a stain on it, so soft that the sails and clouds seemed set into its blue—a great deal depends, she thought, on distance: on whether people are close to us or far away. For her feeling about Mr. Ramsay altered as he sailed farther and farther across the bay. It seemed to be drawn out, stretched thin; he seemed to recede more and more. He and his children seemed to be swallowed by that blue, that distance. But here on the lawn, right beside her, Mr. Carmichael gave a sudden grunt. She laughed. He clawed his book up off the grass and settled himself back in his chair, puffing and blowing like a sea monster. That was quite another matter, because he was so close. And then all was quiet again. Surely they were up by now, she thought, glancing at the house; but nobody showed. Then again, she remembered, they had always vanished the moment a meal ended, off on their own affairs. It all went with this silence, this emptiness, the unreal feeling of early morning. Sometimes things were like that, she thought, pausing for a moment to look at the long glittering windows and the blue plume of smoke: they turned unreal. It was the same when you came back from a journey, or got over an illness—before habit had spun its web across the surface again, you felt that same startling unreality; felt something rise up. Life was never more vivid than then. You could be at your ease. You did not, thank goodness, have to march briskly across the lawn to greet old Mrs. Beckwith as she came out looking for a corner to sit in—“Oh good morning, Mrs. Beckwith! What a lovely day! Are you going to be so bold as to sit in the sun? Jasper’s hidden the chairs. Do let me find you one!”—and all the rest of the usual small talk. You did not have to talk at all. You glided, you shook out your sails (the bay was busy now, with boats setting out), between things and beyond them. It was not empty; it was full to the brim. She seemed to be standing in some substance up to her lips, to move in it, float in it, sink in it—yes, for these waters had no bottom. So many lives had spilled into them. The Ramsays’, the children’s, and all kinds of strays and scraps of things as well. A washerwoman with her basket; a rook; a red-hot poker; the purples and gray-greens of flowers—some shared feeling that held the whole thing together.

For hendes følelse over for hr. Ramsay ændrede sig, efterhånden som han sejlede længere og længere ud over bugten. Den syntes at blive trukket ud, strakt tynd; han syntes at fjerne sig mere og mere. Han og hans børn syntes at blive opslugt af det blå, af den afstand. Men her på plænen, lige ved siden af hende, udstødte hr. Carmichael et pludseligt grynt. Hun lo. Han rev sin bog op fra græsset og satte sig til rette i stolen igen, pustende og stønnende som et havuhyre. Det var noget ganske andet, for han var jo så tæt på. Og så blev alt stille igen. De måtte da være oppe nu, tænkte hun og kastede et blik på huset; men der var ingen at se. Men så huskede hun, at de altid var forsvundet i samme øjeblik, et måltid var slut, af sted i deres egne anliggender. Det hørte alt sammen til denne stilhed, denne tomhed, den uvirkelige følelse af tidlig morgen. Nogle gange var tingene sådan, tænkte hun og standsede et øjeblik for at se på de lange glitrende vinduer og den blå røgsky: de blev uvirkelige. Det var det samme, når man kom hjem fra en rejse eller var kommet sig efter en sygdom — før vanen igen havde spundet sit spind henover overfladen, følte man den samme forbløffende uvirkelighed; følte noget rejse sig. Livet var aldrig mere levende end da. Man kunne være ved sig selv. Man behøvede, gudskelov, ikke at marchere rask hen over plænen for at hilse på gamle fru Beckwith, som kom ud for at finde en krog at sidde i — »Åh, godmorgen, fru Beckwith! Sikke en dejlig dag! Man gled, man rystede sine sejl ud (bugten var travl nu, med både på vej ud), mellem tingene og hinsides dem. Det var ikke tomt; det var fyldt til randen. Hun syntes at stå i en eller anden substans op til læberne, at bevæge sig i den, flyde i den, synke i den — ja, for disse vande havde ingen bund. Så mange liv var løbet ud i dem. Ramsays, børnenes og alle mulige hjemløse småting og stumper af ting ovenikøbet. En vaskekone med sin kurv; en råge; fakkelliljer; blomsternes purpur og grågrønne toner — en eller anden fælles følelse, der holdt det hele sammen.

Was the design wrong, perhaps? Did the line of the wall need breaking up, she wondered? Were the trees too heavy a mass? She gave an ironic smile; hadn’t she believed, when she started, that she had solved her problem?

english: Here on the grass, on the ground, she thought, sitting down and prodding a little colony of plantains with her brush, for the lawn was very rough. Here, sitting on the world, she thought. She could not rid herself of the sense that everything this morning was happening for the first time—perhaps for the last—just as a traveler on a train, even half asleep, knows as he gazes out of the window that he has to look now, because never again will he see that town, or that mule-cart, or that woman working in the fields. The lawn was the world; up here, on this high perch, the two of them were together, she thought, looking over at old Mr. Carmichael, who seemed to share her thoughts (though neither had said a word all this while). And perhaps she would never see him again. He was getting old. And he was getting famous too, she remembered, smiling at the slipper that hung from his foot. People said his poetry was “so beautiful.” They were bringing out things he had written forty years ago. There was a famous man now by the name of Carmichael, she thought with a smile—how many shapes one person could take on! In the newspapers he was that; here he was just as he had always been. He looked the same—a bit grayer, if anything. Yes, the same; and yet somebody had told her, she recalled, that when the news came of Andrew Ramsay’s death (a shell killed him in an instant; he would have been a great mathematician), Mr. Carmichael had “lost all interest in life.” What could that mean? she wondered. Had he gone marching through Trafalgar Square clutching a big stick? Had he sat alone in his room in St. John’s Wood turning page after page without reading a word? She had no idea what he had done when he heard that Andrew was dead, but she sensed it in him all the same. All they ever did was mumble to each other on the stairs, look up at the sky, and say it will be fine or it won’t be fine. Still, this was one way of knowing people, she thought: knowing the outline rather than the detail, the way you might sit in your garden and watch a hillside running purple down into the distant heather. That was how she knew him. She knew that something in him had changed. Not one line of his poetry had she ever read. Yet she felt she knew how it went: slow and sonorous, seasoned and mellow. It was about the desert and the camel, about the palm tree and the sunset. It was utterly impersonal; it had something to say about death and very little about love. He had a kind of aloofness. He asked very little of other people. Hadn’t he always lurched past the drawing-room window rather awkwardly, a newspaper under his arm, trying to dodge Mrs. Ramsay, whom for some reason he did not much like? Which was exactly why, of course, she always tried to make him stop. He would bow to her—pull up unwillingly and bow low. Irritated that he wanted nothing from her, Mrs. Ramsay would ask him (Lily could hear her) wouldn’t he like a coat, a rug, a newspaper? No, there was nothing he wanted. (Here he bowed.) Something in her did not appeal to him. Perhaps it was her masterful way, her certainty, a matter-of-fact streak in her. She was so direct.

Hvilket netop var grunden til, at hun naturligvis altid forsøgte at få ham til at standse. Han ville bukke for hende — standse modstræbende og bukke dybt. english: During the war she had gone into a hall one day and heard him give a speech. He was denouncing something, condemning somebody. He was preaching brotherly love. And all she could feel was: how could he love humanity, this man who could not tell one picture from another—who had stood behind her smoking his shag (“fivepence an ounce, Miss Briscoe”) and made a point of telling her women can’t write, women can’t paint, not so much because he believed it as because, for some odd reason, he wanted it to be so? There he stood on a platform, lean and red and raucous, preaching love (among the plantains ants were crawling, and she disturbed them with her brush—red, busy ants, rather like Charles Tansley). From her seat in the half-empty hall she had watched him ironically as he pumped love into that cold space—and suddenly there was the old barrel, or whatever it had been, bobbing up and down in the waves, and Mrs. Ramsay hunting among the pebbles for her glasses case. “Oh dear! What a nuisance! Lost again. Don’t bother, Mr. Tansley. I lose thousands every summer.” At that he had pressed his chin back against his collar, as though afraid of seeming to approve such exaggeration—but he could put up with it from her, because he liked her—and had smiled very charmingly. He must have confided in her on one of those long excursions when people got separated and walked home alone. He was paying for his little sister’s education, Mrs. Ramsay had told her. It did him enormous credit. Her own picture of him was grotesque, Lily knew perfectly well, stirring the plantains with her brush. After all, half of what you thought about other people was grotesque. Such ideas served private purposes of your own. For her, he stood in for a whipping boy. When she was in a bad mood she caught herself flogging his lean flanks. If she wanted to take him seriously, she had to borrow Mrs. Ramsay’s sayings and see him through her eyes.
danish_before_fix: Under krigen var hun en dag gået ind i en sal og havde hørt ham holde en tale. Han fordømte noget, han dømte nogen. Han prædikede broderkærlighed. Og alt, hvad hun kunne føle, var: hvordan kunne han elske menneskeheden, denne mand, der ikke kunne kende det ene maleri fra det andet — som havde stået bag hende og røget sin shag (»fem pence for en unze, frøken Briscoe«) og lagt vægt på at fortælle hende, at kvinder ikke kan skrive, kvinder ikke kan male, ikke så meget fordi han troede på det, som fordi han af en eller anden underlig grund ønskede, at det skulle være sådan? Der stod han på en talerstol, mager og rød og hæs, og prædikede kærlighed (blandt vejbredplanterne kravlede der myrer, og hun forstyrrede dem med sin pensel — røde, travle myrer, ligesom Charles Tansley). Fra sin plads i den halvtomme sal havde hun iagttaget ham ironisk, mens han pumpede kærlighed ud i det kolde rum — og pludselig var der den gamle tønde, eller hvad det nu havde været, der gyngede op og ned i bølgerne, og fru Ramsay, der ledte blandt strandstenene efter sit brilleetui. »Åh nej! Sikke en plage! Væk igen. Lad være at genere Dem, hr. Tansley. Jeg mister tusindvis hver sommer.« Ved det havde han trykket hagen tilbage mod flippen, som om han var bange for at synes at billige en sådan overdrivelse — men fra hende kunne han udholde det, fordi han kunne lide hende — og havde smilet meget indtagende. Han måtte have betroet sig til hende på en af de lange udflugter, hvor folk blev adskilt og gik alene hjem. Han betalte for sin lillesøsters uddannelse, havde fru Ramsay fortalt hende. Det gjorde ham stor ære. Hendes eget billede af ham var grotesk, vidste Lily udmærket, mens hun rørte i vejbredplanterne med sin pensel. Når alt kom til alt, var halvdelen af, hvad man tænkte om andre mennesker, grotesk. Sådanne forestillinger tjente ens egne private formål. For hende stod han i stedet for en syndebuk. Når hun var i dårligt humør, opdagede hun, at hun piskede hans magre flanker. Hvis hun ville tage ham alvorligt, måtte hun låne fru Ramsays ord og se ham med hendes øjne.
